exhaustive

/ig-ZOS-tiv/ — rhymes with "positive" · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something exhaustive covers every possible detail or option, leaving nothing out.

After an exhaustive search of every drawer and pocket, she found the ring in her shoe.

Example

After an exhaustive search of every drawer and pocket, she found the ring in her shoe.

The word exhaustive means leaving nothing out or covering every possible detail. In this sentence, she searched every single location—every drawer and every pocket—making the search truly exhaustive. A plainer word like "thorough" would work, but it doesn't emphasize as strongly that every possibility was checked. Exhaustive specifies that nothing at all was overlooked.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

complete: Complete says that every part is present and the job is finished — a complete set, a complete draft. Exhaustive describes how the work was done: every possibility examined, nothing overlooked. A review can be complete the moment it ends; only one that checked every single file is exhaustive.

painstaking: Painstaking describes the care and effort put in — painstaking work is done slowly and carefully, as if taking pains over every step. Exhaustive measures coverage instead: whether every possibility was checked. A painstaking restorer may work on a single corner for weeks; an exhaustive catalog lists every work.

systematic: Systematic means following an organized plan, step by step in a fixed order. Exhaustive is a claim about coverage, not method: nothing at all was left out. A systematic search can be called off halfway and stay systematic, but no search that skips anything can be called exhaustive.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

superficial: touching only the surface, not deep

cursory: hasty and quick, skipping the details

Where it sits · how completely everything is covered

cursory → thorough → comprehensive → exhaustive

cursory vs. exhaustive: Cursory is the weakest word on this scale and the opposite of exhaustive: a cursory look skims the surface, while an exhaustive one misses nothing.

thorough vs. exhaustive: Thorough is strong, but exhaustive is stronger — a thorough check is careful, while an exhaustive check covers every single possibility.

comprehensive vs. exhaustive: Comprehensive comes close to exhaustive, but exhaustive goes further still: comprehensive covers a wide range, while exhaustive leaves absolutely nothing out.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-: out, off (Latin)

Root — haust: to draw up, drain (Latin haurire) (Latin)

Suffix — -ive: tending to (adjective-forming) (Latin)

Put it together: Ex- ('out') + haust ('draw up, drain') + -ive: an exhaustive effort 'draws out' every last possibility until the subject is completely drained — nothing is left unexamined.

Use the root in a new word: exhaust: If you exhaust your allowance, you draw it down until nothing is left — and an exhaustive search likewise draws out every last possibility.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / academic

Use exhaustive when you want to emphasize that every detail or possibility was covered, leaving absolutely nothing out. It's more formal and emphatic than "thorough" and suggests a definitive, comprehensive treatment. For casual situations ("thorough cleaning"), just use "thorough."
